title: Prompting LLMs: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on zero-shot and few-shot prompting, system prompts, chain-of-thought, structured output, sampling controls (temperature, top-p) and prompt injection risks, from mental model to a final cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Prompting Mental Model
points: A prompt is the only input that steers a frozen model: the model predicts the next tokens given your text, so clearer context gives better output
Zero-shot: instruction only, no examples; works for common tasks like summarise or translate
Few-shot: 2-5 worked input→output examples in the prompt (in-context learning); no weights change
Prompt anatomy: role/system, task instruction, context/data, examples, output format
Prompts are not deterministic code: same prompt can give different outputs, so test on a set of cases, not one try

chapters.title: Core Workflow: Zero-Shot to Few-Shot
points: Start zero-shot with a specific instruction, audience and output format; add examples only if output misses the target
Pick examples that cover edge cases and label variety; keep them consistent in format
Order and balance matter: skewed labels or the last example can bias the answer (recency bias)
Delimit sections with tags or ### so instructions, data and examples are not confused
Iterate loop: write prompt → run on 5-10 test inputs → inspect failures → change one thing → rerun

chapters.title: System Prompts and Chain-of-Thought
points: System prompt sets persistent role, rules, tone and constraints; the user message carries the per-request task
Put hard rules in the system prompt as short, specific, testable statements (e.g. 'answer in max 3 sentences'), not vague wishes
Chain-of-thought (CoT): ask the model to reason step by step before the final answer; helps math, logic, multi-step tasks
Zero-shot CoT = add 'Think step by step'; few-shot CoT = examples that include the reasoning
CoT costs more tokens and latency, and is unneeded for simple lookups; many reasoning models already think internally, so don't over-instruct

chapters.title: Structured Output and Sampling Controls
points: Structured output: request JSON matching a schema, give one example, and use the API's JSON mode / schema-constrained or tool-call output when available
Always validate parsed output (json.loads plus schema check) and retry or repair on failure; never trust raw text
Temperature scales randomness: 0 to ~0.3 for extraction, classification and code; 0.7 to 1 for brainstorming and creative writing
Top-p (nucleus sampling) samples only from the smallest token set whose probability sums to p; tune temperature or top-p, not both
Low temperature is not a guarantee of determinism or correctness; it only makes outputs more repeatable and can still be confidently wrong

chapters.title: Prompt Injection and Common Mistakes
points: Prompt injection: untrusted text (user input, web page, email, document) contains instructions that override yours; indirect injection hides them in retrieved content
The model cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so a system-prompt warning like 'ignore attacks' is not a defence
Mitigate: delimit and label untrusted data, least-privilege tools, human approval for sensitive actions, and filter or validate outputs
Never put secrets in prompts and never let model output run as code, SQL or shell without checks
Common mistakes: vague instructions, too many examples, conflicting rules, no test set, changing several things at once

chapters.title: Prompting Cheat Sheet
points: Order of attack: zero-shot → add format → few-shot → CoT → structured output
Few-shot: 2-5 diverse, consistently formatted examples; mind label balance and last-example bias
System prompt = persistent role and rules; user prompt = this request
CoT for reasoning tasks; skip for simple ones; costs tokens
Temperature 0-0.3 deterministic tasks, 0.7-1 creative; adjust one of temperature or top-p
Treat all external text as untrusted; least privilege plus validate output
